caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001341
attempts.entry_title: Barrel cortex activity during tactile VR navigation decisions (Armstrong and Vlasov 2026)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Armstrong and Vlasov (2026) on dandiset 001341, which holds two of the paper's 19 animals (489 and 503), with spike-sorted units, the trials table and the ball tracking. The behaviour is on the clock of the trials table and its claims are tested; the spike times are not, and the files hold no synchronisation signal, so the neural claims that need spike timing are blocked. Whisker, touch, wall and gait data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Armstrong and Vlasov (2026) from dandiset 001341

outcomes.statement: The recordings comprise 13 ephys sessions and 6 behaviour-only sessions, one per animal, with the numbers of accepted single units and of trials per animal listed in Table S1, and with the units and OL turn trials of the example sessions given in Fig. 1J-K and Fig. S4.
outcomes.source: SI Appendix, Table S1; Fig. 1J-K legend; Fig. S4 legend
outcomes.inferred: Numbers read from Table S1 and the legends of Fig. 1J-K and Fig. S4; no sentence states them together.
outcomes.notes: The dataset holds 2 of the 19 animals of Table S1 (489 and 503, 2 of 13 ephys sessions), so 17 trial counts and 11 unit counts cannot be compared. Neither unit count present matches (489 61 against 65, 503 43 against 48), nor either OL count (489 249 OL_L and 251 OL_R in its labelled rows against 266 and 265; 503 230 and 283 against 305 and 304). The total trial counts match (503 1027 rows against 1027; 489 1000 labelled rows against 1000, though its table has 1611 rows, of which rows 1000 to 1610 repeat one row). That the 1000 intact rows of 489 are the trials of Table S1 is an assumption; counted with its 611 repeated rows, 489 has 1611 trials, outside 10% of 1000, and its OL counts are 298 OL_L and 507 OL_R when the 305 repeated turns are given the direction of their displacement at 1 s. For 489 the layer counts differ from Fig. 5B in L2/3 (7 against 10) and L6 (12 against 13), and the FS and RS counts by the 0.4 ms rule are 30 and 31 against 43 and 22. The header's inconsistencies of the paper (634 against 668 units, the trial counts of 489 and 503 in different figures) cannot be settled from two animals.
deviations: Only animals 489 and 503 are in the dataset.

For 489 the trials are counted on the first 1000 rows, whose labels and times are usable; the 611 rows after them repeat one row of the table. That these 1000 rows are the 1000 trials of Table S1 is an assumption; the count of all 1611 rows is also given.

outcomes.statement: In the C2 principal barrel column, population spiking across all layers is strongly and synchronously modulated during OL turns, in five consecutive epochs (stable spiking, a sharp peak, suppression, a ramp for contralateral turns, and a return to stable spiking).
outcomes.source: Results, Population dynamics in C2 barrel column..., paragraph 2; Fig. 1J-O
outcomes.quote: Spiking activity across all cortical layers is strongly modulated during navigation decisions and can roughly be divided into five consecutive epochs
outcomes.notes: The spike times are not on the clock of the trials table and the files hold no synchronisation signal, though the SI says TTL signals were used to synchronise them. At the stored onsets the population rate of 489 shows no trial-locked response (5.8 to 8.7 Hz over -1 to 2 s, suppression-window minimum at least 86% of baseline), and trial type cannot be decoded from per-unit spike counts (0.460 to 0.522 against shuffled 95th percentiles of 0.535 to 0.542), while lateral position decodes it at 0.954. In 489 the onset-triggered lag search exceeds the 95th percentile of its null in 2 of 12 windows, though its best lags rise almost steadily over windows 0 to 6 (4.36 to 12.23 s), which suggests a drifting offset; the running-speed correlations are weak (|r| at most 0.17), so no clock can be fitted, and any clock from these lags would be no finer than that of 503. In 503 a clock fitted from running speed (lag 11.86 s plus 1.37 ms per s) recovers direction-specific responses and trial type decodes at 0.865 to 0.912, but the clock has a residual SD of 0.56 s and also decodes trial type before the onset (0.655), far coarser than the 5 to 180 ms windows the claim tests. The clock was fitted to running speed, and 503 runs in 1.7% of OL_L and 31.8% of OL_R rows, so the responses and decoding on it may in part reflect running. An alignment fitted to the neural response would set the timings the claim tests, so none was adopted.

outcomes.statement: For animal 489, the population rate is about 2 Hz during straight running before the turn, peaks sharply at t = 0.026 s (epoch 2), drops to about 0.7 Hz (epoch 3) for both turn directions, and, for contralateral turns only, ramps to a maximum at about t = 0.25 s (epoch 4); for ipsilateral turns the suppression lasts to the end of the turn.
outcomes.source: Results, Population dynamics in C2 barrel column..., paragraph 2; Fig. 1N
outcomes.quote: the stable spiking (t < 0 s, 2 ± 0.1 Hz, mean ± SD) of epoch 1 during CL straight running is disrupted by a sharp peak we refer as epoch 2 (t = 0.026 s) ... Epoch 3 follows, which exhibits strong suppression of spiking activity down to 0.7 ± 0.1 Hz (mean ± SD) for both left and right turns ... While for ipsilateral turns the suppression lasts until the turn end ... contralateral turns produce a strong ramping activity labeled as epoch 4, (t = 0.25 s
outcomes.notes: The epoch 1 population rate of 489 is 6.65 to 7.80 Hz under reading (a) (-0.5 to 0 s) and 6.74 to 7.75 Hz under reading (b) (-1 to 0 s), for OL_L and OL_R, with the onsets shifted by each of 801 lags from -20 to 60 s; none of the 1602 (lag, turn) pairs is within 2.0 ± 0.1 Hz. Measured is reading (a), OL_L, at the stored onsets. Over all CL rows the rate per unit is 7.18 to 7.26 Hz at lags of 0 to 25 s, and 7.09 Hz over the whole recording; the units table gives a mean firing rate of 5.91 Hz (median 2.95 Hz, 19 of 61 units below 2 Hz). The epoch 2 peak time, the epoch 3 minimum and the epoch 4 maximum time need spikes on the trial clock, which the files do not give (see fig1lm-staged-modulation), and are not tested.
deviations: The spike times are not on the trial clock, so the epoch 1 rate is computed at every lag from -20 to 60 s in 0.1 s steps, the range searched in the data check, and the three timed values are not tested.
The dataset has 61 units for 489 and 249 and 251 labelled OL_L and OL_R trials, where the paper has 65 units and 266 and 265 trials.

outcomes.statement: All five epochs dominate the activity of every one of the 65 simultaneously recorded units of animal 489, reproducibly across 531 randomized trials with a jitter of about 30 ms.
outcomes.source: Results, Population dynamics in C2 barrel column..., paragraph 2; Fig. 1J-K; Fig. S5
outcomes.quote: all five epochs are major features that dominate the activity for all 65 simultaneously recorded units ... highly reproducible across 531 randomized trials with jitter of just 30 ms
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation). The dataset has 61 units for 489, not 65, and 249 and 251 labelled OL_L and OL_R trials, not 266 and 265.

outcomes.statement: For animal 489 the linear slope of the epoch 4 ramp in contralateral (OL_L) trials is 12.25 (12.25 ± 0.88, mean ± SEM, in Fig. 4B; 12.25 ± 0.76 in Fig. 1N).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping neural activity reflects temporal accumulation..., paragraph 2; Fig. 4B bottom; Discussion, paragraph 2; Fig. 1N
outcomes.quote: This is noticeably close to the linear slope of ramping peak 4 of 12.25 ± 0.88 (mean ± SEM)
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation).

outcomes.statement: At the end of the turn, when the contralateral wall moves back out at t = 1.8 s, the contralateral population shows a peak (2'), a longer suppression with ramp onset at t = 2.0 s, and a slower ramp (4') that peaks at t = 2.58 s with a slope of 2.05, about 7 times smaller than the slope of the first ramp.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 2; Fig. 1O; Results, Stages of decision-making..., paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Epoch 3′ suppression is significantly longer with the onset of ramping activity at t = 2.0 s (0.21 s delay) suggesting regulation of integration onset to task demand. Ramping in epoch 4′ is much slower reaching maximum at t = 2.58 s (0.78 s delay). The fitted linear slope (2.05 ± 0.05, mean ± SEM, black triangle in Fig. 1O ) is 7× smaller than for the first turn at trial start (12.25 ± 0.76, mean ± SEM, triangle Fig. 1N )
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation), and depends on fig1n-ramp-slope.

outcomes.statement: The ramps of epochs 4 and 4' appear only in contralateral (OL_L) turns, while the epoch 2 and 2' peaks appear for both turn directions, showing strong lateralization.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 5; Fig. 1J-O; Fig. 5C-D
outcomes.quote: While epochs 2 (at trial start) and 2′ (at trial end) are present for both left and right turns, the ramping in epochs 4 and 4′ is exclusively presented only for contralateral left turn trials indicating extraordinarily strong lateralization
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation). Of the seven animals of the criterion only 489 and 503 are in the dataset (data_missing for the other five). On the coarse speed clock of 503 (residual SD 0.56 s) the population rate rises by 1.38 Hz in 0 to 0.3 s for OL_L and falls by 0.82 Hz for OL_R (null -0.22 to +0.25 Hz), which may in part reflect running (1.7% of OL_L and 31.8% of OL_R rows run), but the criterion's windows (0.065 to 0.25 s) are far shorter than the clock's error, and 489 has no clock.

outcomes.statement: Mice run at fast speeds, 21 ± 4 cm/s (mean ± SD).
outcomes.source: Results, Ethological decision-making..., paragraph 1; SI Fig. S1A; SI Animal preparation
outcomes.quote: running at fast speeds (21 ± 4 cm/s, mean ± SD
outcomes.notes: Animal 503 runs at a mean of 5.93 cm/s over all samples (reading a) and 12.95 cm/s over the samples of its running trials (reading b), outside 21 ± 4 cm/s. Reading (c) has 2 of 19 animals; their mean running speed is 16.56 cm/s, also outside, though 489 alone (19.98) is inside. Against Table S1, 489 matches (19.98 against 22.2 cm/s, 91.7% running trials against 92.6%) and 503 does not (13.14 against 16.1 cm/s, 27.7% against 52.8%). By row type 503 runs in 37.0% of its CL rows, 1.7% of its OL_L rows and 31.8% of its OL_R rows, so no choice of rows gives 52.8%; with its unit and OL counts below the paper's, this suggests that the deposited session or curation of 503 differs from the one the paper analysed. The dataset holds no habituation sessions (reading d).
deviations: Reading (c) uses the 2 animals in the dataset where the criterion has 19.

outcomes.statement: In the unrewarded task, with a correct trial defined as ±1 cm lateral clearance at t = 1 s, animal 503 succeeds in 95% of 414 randomized turn trials (14 failed trajectories).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral correlates of decision-making..., paragraph 1; Fig. 2A
outcomes.quote: Defining threshold for correct trials as ±1 cm lateral clearance at t = 1 s, the success rate reaches 95% (14 failed red trajectories in Fig. 2A
outcomes.notes: Under the eight readings of the criterion the success rate of 503 is 0.609 to 0.694, with 154 to 165 failed trials, against 0.95 and 14; measured is reading (e), (a), (c), 0.680 with 164 failures of 513. The failures are trials with almost no lateral movement (5th percentile of displacement in the turn direction at 1 s is 0.00 cm). In a variant outside the criterion, the 94 OL trials run above 10 cm/s succeed at 0.979 to 1.000 (0 to 2 failures), so the paper's 414 trials may be a selection of running trials that it does not describe. These 94 trials are almost all OL_R, as 503 runs in 1.7% of its 230 OL_L rows and 31.8% of its 283 OL_R rows.
deviations: The dataset has 513 OL trials for 503 (230 OL_L, 283 OL_R); the paper's 414 cannot be identified among them.

outcomes.statement: Lateral positions are tightly confined during the straight CL section (0.14 ± 0.55 cm, mean ± SD, at t = 0) and their distribution widens over time after the turn (t = 1 s and 3 s), about twice as wide at 3 s as at 2 s (SD 2.30 against 1.49).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral correlates of decision-making..., paragraph 1; Fig. 2B; Discussion, paragraph 2; Fig. S6B
outcomes.quote: While the straight CL section produces trajectories tightly confined within 0.14 cm ± 0.55 (mean ± SD) ... distributions of lateral distances after the turn widen over time ... (2.30 SD at 3 s trial time vs. 1.49 SD at 2 s time for Fig. 2 B , Top , and SI Appendix , Fig. S6 B , Top )
outcomes.notes: The stored lateral distance restarts at 0 at each trial, so under reading (a) it is 0.00 ± 0.00 cm at t = 0 by construction. Integrated from the start of the straight section (reading b, given as measured with reading c), 503 is at 0.20 ± 0.84 cm at t = 0; the mean is within tolerance, the SD (0.84 against 0.55 ± 0.055) is not. The distribution widens under (b) (503 SD 0.84, 2.90 and 7.20 cm at 0, 1 and 3 s), but no reading gives the 2 s and 3 s SDs of 1.49 and 2.30 (503 7.02 and 7.20, 489 4.06 and 5.40 under b; 503 0.76 at 3 s and 489 3.50 at 2 s under a). Every trial has a value at 1, 2 and 3 s, and all but one of 489 at 0 s. Per turn direction the 503 SDs at 3 s are 4.58 (OL_L) and 3.10 (OL_R) under (b).
deviations: Following the legends, 503 pools OL_L and OL_R (Fig. 2B) and 489 uses OL_L (Fig. S6A-B), 249 labelled OL_L trials where the paper has 520.
The dataset holds no wall positions, so lateral position relative to the corridor cannot be computed; the readings use the ball's lateral displacement.

outcomes.statement: The success rate rises steeply as the approaching wall comes closer to the snout, from 8 mm (whisker barely touching) to 1 mm (whisker strongly bent).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral correlates of decision-making..., paragraph 1; Fig. 2C; Fig. S6E-G
outcomes.quote: The resulting success rate as a function of wall distance ( Fig. 2C ) exhibits a strong increase toward shorter distances
outcomes.notes: The psychometric animals (474, 475, 499, 518) are not in the dataset, and neither session in it varies the OL wall distance or records it. The paper names no other archive for these data.

outcomes.statement: Turns are steeper (larger mean turn angle) when the wall comes closer.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral correlates of decision-making..., paragraph 1; Fig. 2D
outcomes.quote: Better threshold clearance is achieved by steeper turn angles ( Fig. 2D ) at closer wall distances
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig2c-psychometric; the same animals and wall distances are missing.

outcomes.statement: During straight CL running the C2 whisker whisks at 15 ± 2 Hz with an amplitude of 39 ± 5 degrees around a set point of 58 ± 5 degrees; once the wall is close (t > 0.2 s) the whisker angle is clamped at 68 ± 12 degrees.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral correlates of decision-making..., paragraph 2; Fig. 2E-F
outcomes.quote: Whisking during CL straight run (t < 0) is executed at 15 ± 2 Hz (mean ± SD) with an amplitude of just 39 ± 5° (mean ± SD) around a set point of 58 ± 5° (mean ± SD) ... (whisker angle clamped at 68° ± 12 (mean ± SD) for t > 0.2 s
outcomes.notes: The files hold no whisker tracking (angle, curvature or touches), and animals 573 and 589 are not in the dataset.

outcomes.statement: The choice period lasts 0.32 s, between the mean first whisker touch of the approaching wall (0.06 ± 0.03 s) and the mean reaction time defined by the stereotypic hind-leg push (0.38 ± 0.07 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral correlates of decision-making..., paragraph 3; Fig. 2I
outcomes.quote: Corresponding time histograms for FT and RT ( Fig. 2I ) indicate the choice period of 0.32 s between the mean FT (0.06 ± 0.03 s, mean ± SD) and mean RT (0.38 ± 0.07 s, mean ± SD)
outcomes.notes: First touch needs whisker touch times, which are not in the dataset, and animals 573 and 480 are not in it. Reaction times under the claim's readings are reported for 489 and 503 in the fig4-ddm-fit section (489 OL_L means 0.297 to 0.352 s; 503 OL_L 0.296 to 0.879 s), as the criterion asks.

outcomes.statement: During straight CL running, over 80% of units encode more than one behavioural or sensory variable (whisking kinetics and kinematics, speed, gait), and the wall feedback signal V_wall is among the strongest encoded variables.
outcomes.source: Results, Stages of decision-making..., paragraph 2; Fig. 2J-K; SI Multiparameter GLM regression
outcomes.quote: In fact, multidimensional tuning is characteristic for the majority of population (over 80% of units, Fig. 2K ) ... Unsurprisingly, among the strongest correlations is the feedback signal V wall
outcomes.notes: Animal 579 is not in the dataset, and the files hold none of the whisking, gait or wall regressors.

outcomes.statement: The epoch 2 peaks appear within 10 ms of the first whisker touch, consistent with the afferent delay from follicle to barrel cortex, which marks them as sensory (mismatch) signals.
outcomes.source: Results, Stages of decision-making..., paragraph 3; Fig. 1N-O; Fig. 2F
outcomes.quote: In all cases, epoch 2 peaks appear within 10 ms range from FT, which is consistent with the expected afferent delay from whisker follicle to barrel cortex
outcomes.notes: Needs whisker touch times, which are not in the dataset; it also needs spikes on the trial clock, which the files do not give (see fig1lm-staged-modulation).

outcomes.statement: The epoch 4 ramp dominates the response only when the animal is actively running; during brief stops with active whisking the epoch 2 peak dominates and the ramp is absent.
outcomes.source: Results, Stages of decision-making..., paragraph 4; Fig. 2L
outcomes.quote: peak 4 activity dominates the modulation only when the animal is actively navigating
outcomes.notes: The claim is judged on animal 480, which is not in the dataset. The variant on other animals needs spikes on the trial clock, which the files do not give (see fig1lm-staged-modulation).

outcomes.statement: Population activity is high-dimensional during epoch 1 and collapses to a single dimension after first touch during epochs 2 to 4, staying one-dimensional through the choice period and rising again at decision execution and in epoch 5.
outcomes.source: Results, Stages of decision-making..., paragraph 5; Fig. 2M; SI Dimensionality reduction
outcomes.quote: confirms the high-dimensional neural coding during epoch 1 that collapses rapidly to just a single dimension following the FT during epochs 2, 3, and 4 ... the neural population remains one-dimensional ( 46 ) during choice period between FT and RT and starts to increase only at the onset of decision execution and later, in epoch 5
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset at 1 ms resolution (see fig1lm-staged-modulation).

outcomes.statement: Fitted separately to CL straight running and to OL turn decisions, the GLM shows that most units lose during the decision the significant tuning to sensory and behavioural variables they show during straight running (epoch 1).
outcomes.source: Results, Stages of decision-making..., paragraph 5; SI Fig. S12B-C
outcomes.quote: When analyzed with reduced GLM (examples in SI Appendix , Fig. S12 B and C ), the majority of units show no significant tuning for both sensory and behavioral variables during decision that they previously exhibited during epoch 1
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig2jk-glm-mixed-tuning; the GLM's whisking, gait and wall regressors are not in the dataset.

outcomes.statement: At turn onset the wall retracts to its maximum 12 mm distance within a mean of 11 ms, so most (>80%) first touches are on the approaching wall; during the epoch 3 suppression the wall approaches from 8.7 to 4.4 mm, and it reaches its final 2 mm position at 200 ms.
outcomes.source: Results, Could the neural activity modulation be explained by simple sensory drive?, paragraphs 2 and 3; Fig. 3A, 3P-Q
outcomes.quote: The wall retracts very rapidly ( Fig. 3P ), reaching the maximum 12 mm distance at a mean delay as fast as 11 ms. Therefore, the majority (>80%) of first whisker touch (FT) events ( Fig. 3Q ) correspond to whisker palpating approaching ... when the wall is not retracting but fast approaching from 8.7 mm to 4.4 mm ... at a constant speed until the final position of 2 mm is reached at 200 ms
outcomes.notes: The files hold no wall positions or touch times, and animal 589 is not in the dataset.

outcomes.statement: The whisker touches the wall about 48 ± 4% of the time, in touches of median duration 21 ms; touch probability increases during epoch 4, reaching 90% in epoch 5.
outcomes.source: Results, Could the neural activity modulation be explained by simple sensory drive?, paragraph 3; Fig. 3B-D, 3M-O
outcomes.quote: The whisker stays in direct contact with the wall about 48 ± 4% of the time ( Fig. 3C ) with median touch duration of 21 ms ... Whisker touch probability ( Fig. 3C ) increases monotonously during epoch 4, as does mean whisker curvature ( Fig. 3D ), reaching 90% in epoch 5
outcomes.notes: The files hold no touch annotations, and animal 589 is not in the dataset.

outcomes.statement: Across epochs 1, 2-3 and 4-5 the whisker palpates the wall at a constant 15 ± 2 Hz, with statistically identical amplitudes, set angles and per-cycle curvature maxima.
outcomes.source: Results, Could the neural activity modulation be explained by simple sensory drive?, paragraph 3; Fig. 3I-L
outcomes.quote: The whisker palpates the wall at a constant 15 ± 2 Hz frequency ( Fig. 3I ), with statistically identical amplitudes ( Fig. 3J ), and set angles ( Fig. 3K ) ... producing periodically modulated curvature with statistically identical maximum per each cycle ( Fig. 3L )

statistics.about: whisking amplitude across epoch groups (Fig. 3J legend), a result that contradicts the text
whisking set angle across epoch groups (Fig. 3K legend)
per-cycle maximum curvature across epoch groups (Fig. 3L legend)

outcomes.notes: The files hold no whisker tracking, and animal 589 is not in the dataset.

outcomes.statement: While sensory input is monotonous during the turn (constant whisking, wall contact rising steadily), neural activity is highly nonstationary (peak, suppression, ramp, return), so the modulation is not explained by simple sensory drive.
outcomes.source: Results, Could the neural activity modulation be explained by simple sensory drive?, paragraph 3; Fig. 3
outcomes.quote: However, while sensory input is monotonous, in stark contrast to the “simple sensory drive” hypothesis, the neural activity is highly nonstationary
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig3c-touch-statistics (touch data missing) and on fig1lm-staged-modulation (blocked, metadata_insufficient).

outcomes.statement: A classical drift-diffusion model fitted to the reaction-time distribution of animal 489 gives a nondecision time of 0.12 s, drift 2.91, bound 0.59 and noise 0.25 (BIC -664); a generalized DDM with collapsing bounds and leak fits better (BIC -705), with normalized drift K/B of 11.12.
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping neural activity reflects temporal accumulation..., paragraph 1; Fig. 4B-E; SI Table S2
outcomes.quote: Fitting classical DDM ( Materials and Methods ) to experimental distribution of RT ( Fig. 4B ) produces best fit (Bayesian information criterion, BIC of −664, Fig. 4C ) for nondecision time (NDT) of 0.12 s ( Fig. 4D ), drift K = 2.91, bound B = 0.59 ( Fig. 4E ), and noise σ = 0.25 ... that produce a better fit (BIC of −705). Normalized drift K/B that defines the time needed to reach the bound in absence of noise and decay is 11.12
outcomes.notes: No reading gives a DDM nondecision time within 0.108 to 0.132 s. It is 0.000 to 0.005 s with all RTs kept, 0.000 to 0.039 s with a uniform mixture and 0.080 to 0.094 s with RTs below 0.1 s dropped (16 fits each). The GDDM BIC is below the DDM BIC in all 4 readings fitted with all RTs kept (-201.6 to -76.8 against 42.7 to 82.8) and with RTs below 0.1 s dropped (-441.5 to -343.8 against -298.4 to -266.4), and in none of the 4 with the mixture (-432.9 to -298.5 against -441.8 to -300.0), so only the GDDM condition holds. The NDT is poorly determined. With all RTs kept it sits under the smallest RT (0.007 s); with a cutoff it lies 0.011 to 0.030 s under the smallest RT kept, so one of 16 cutoff fits (0.129 s, cutoff 0.15 s) is within tolerance because of the cutoff; with the mixture it stays at 0.000 to 0.039 s (0.003 to 0.028 s with a weight up to 0.3) and the mixture weight is at its limit of 0.1 in all 16 DDM fits; with a limit of 0.3 it is 0.158 to 0.243, below the limit but far above the 3 to 5% of RTs below 0.1 s, which suggests the plain DDM misfits the shape of the RT distribution more broadly. In the likelihood profile, NDT fixed at 0.12 s gives a BIC 4.4 above the best, at 0 s; with equal parameter counts this is a deviance difference, so 0.12 s lies just outside a 95% profile-likelihood interval (p about 0.04). The partial outcome rests on the assumption about early RTs; under the mixture handling the GDDM condition fails too, and the claim would be not reproduced. Confidence in this outcome is low. Measured is the first reading, all RTs kept, run angle derivative, 0 to 1 s, clearance in the turn direction, sigma 0.25, with K/B from the GDDM. The other values are far from the paper's; DDM BIC -441.8 to 205.9 over the three handlings (-664, none within tolerance), GDDM BIC at best -441.5 (-705), B within tolerance in 1 of 48 DDM fits, K/B 0.30 to 4.06 (11.12). K is within tolerance in 6, 4 and 0 of 16 fits under the three handlings; with sigma free K, B and sigma are identified only up to a common scale. The GDDM leak is at the -10 edge of its range in all four fits with all RTs kept, 2.50 to 8.17 with the mixture and 6.04 to 9.99 with the cutoff (two of four near the +10 edge).
deviations: The 249 labelled OL_L trials of 489 are used; the paper's 266 (Fig. 4B) or 520 (Fig. S7C-D) cannot be identified among the dataset's trials.
RT maxima at the edge of the search window are not peaks and those trials are dropped (2 to 5 of 249), a standard choice.

Early RTs. Between 8 and 13 RTs per reading fall below 0.1 s, before the leg push the SI says the peak marks (SI, Fitting of drift diffusion models), and the paper's RT histogram of 489 (Fig. S7D) has none below about 0.2 s. The paper does not say how they were handled, so each fit is run with all RTs kept, with a uniform mixture of weight up to 0.1 (PyDDM's OverlayUniformMixture, which its documentation gives to confer robustness in likelihood fits), and with RTs below 0.1 s dropped (an assumption). Fits with cutoffs of 0.05 to 0.2 s and a mixture limit of 0.3 are shown as checks, not readings, since a cutoff sets the NDT.

The GDDM was fitted only under sigma 0.25 and the 0 to 1 s window (4 of 16 readings per handling); as the NDT condition fails in every reading, fits in the other readings could not change the outcome.

The GDDM leak, collapse and fitting ranges, the time step and the loss (PyDDM's BIC) are standard choices; the paper names the components but not their parameterisation (Results, Ramping neural activity, paragraph 1).

outcomes.statement: The DDM nondecision time (0.12 s) matches the 0.12 s onset of the epoch 4 ramp, and the normalized drift (11.12) is close to the ramp's slope (12.25), so the ramp is consistent with accumulation of evidence to a bound.
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping neural activity reflects temporal accumulation..., paragraphs 1 and 2; Fig. 4B
outcomes.quote: appreciable NDT = 0.12 s from both DDM and full DDM ( Fig. 4D ) fits well to the 0.12 s delay of experimentally observed ramping onset at end of epoch 3 for this example animal
outcomes.notes: The ramp onset needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation); it also depends on fig1n-ramp-slope, blocked for the same reason. The DDM part is in fig4-ddm-fit (NDT 0.000 to 0.094 s over three handlings of early RTs).

outcomes.statement: Across seven animals, the epoch 4 ramp slope is 13.05 ± 4.59 (mean ± SD).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping neural activity reflects temporal accumulation..., paragraph 2; Fig. 5E; Fig. S9
outcomes.quote: (other examples in SI Appendix , Fig. S9 and Fig. 5E below, n = 7, 13.05 ± 4.59, mean ± SD)
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation), and 5 of its 7 animals are not in the dataset (data_missing).

outcomes.statement: For an example high-rate unit (489101), the Fano factor is 0.74 ± 0.04 in epochs 1 and 2 and drops to 0.29 at the epoch 4 peak (t = 0.23 s) as total variance saturates, and its VarCE rises quickly at the start of epoch 4 (0.12 to 0.17 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Ramping neural activity reflects temporal accumulation..., paragraph 3; Fig. 4F; SI Analysis of VarCE, paragraph 2; Fig. S10A
outcomes.quote: results in a Fano factor (Fig.S10A, top, black) of 0.74±0.04 (mean ± s.d.). Total variance saturates midway through a strong increase of mean firing rate during ramping that results in a Fano factor dropping down to 0.29 at the peak of epoch 4 at t=0.23s
outcomes.notes: Needs spikes aligned to the turn onset (see fig1lm-staged-modulation). Unit 101 of 489 is in the dataset, the session's highest-rate unit (37.6 Hz), labelled Inhibitory, layer 5A, with a 0.2 ms waveform (FS), where the paper calls 489101 RS.

outcomes.statement: Population VarCE increases linearly between decision onset (0.12 s) and decision termination (0.18 s), whether computed over all units, without outliers, or on residuals, and then declines to a minimum at t = 0.23 s when the decision is executed.

outcomes.quote: When VarCE is calculated from residuals ( 5 , 51 ) ( Materials and Methods ), it is similar ( Fig. 4G , black) showing linear increase between decision onset ( Fig. 4G , up arrow) and decision termination ( Fig. 4G , down arrow) times. VarCE exhibits a fast decline at decision end, reaching minimum at t = 0.23 when the decision is executed

outcomes.statement: The CorCE matrix, computed on residuals, shows correlation rising with time along the diagonal and decaying with time lag along a row, a pattern that disappears when bins are shuffled, as expected for a diffusion process.

outcomes.quote: The calculated ( Materials and Methods ) CorCE matrix ( Fig. 4J ) indeed exhibits characteristic increase of correlation as a function of time and, for given time (e.g., along the top row), shows sequential decay as often observed ( 5 , 51 ) during decision-making. This correlation disappears when bins are randomly shuffled

outcomes.statement: Trial-by-trial streak index analysis during ramping shows random local spike count fluctuations with close to zero mean (0.06 ± 1.36, mean ± SD), indicating a gradual, not step-like, transition in each trial.

outcomes.statement: All epochs, including the suppression and ramp of epochs 3 and 4, are present in layer 4 FS and RS units and in the units of every cortical layer and of each cell class, so the modulation is not confined to a subpopulation.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 3; Fig. 5B

findings.statement: The spike times are not on the clock of the trials table and the behaviour, and the files hold no synchronisation signal or offset (processing, analysis and stimulus are empty), though the SI says LabVIEW TTL signals were used to synchronise the recordings with the behaviour. At the stored turn onsets neither session shows a trial-locked population response, and turn type cannot be decoded from the units' spike counts, while the animal's lateral position decodes it at 0.92 to 0.95. In 503 the lag of the best correlation between spike rate and running speed grows smoothly from 12.9 to 19.75 s over the first 5200 s; a line through it (11.86 s plus 1.37 ms per s, residual SD 0.56 s) recovers trial-locked, turn-specific responses, so the spike times of 503 appear to be about 12 s later than the trial times of the same events, with a gap growing by about 1.4 ms per s. That clock is fitted to running speed, and 503 runs in 1.7% of OL_L and 31.8% of OL_R rows, so the turn-specific responses on it may in part reflect running. In 489 the onset-triggered best lags rise from 4.36 to 12.23 s over the first seven windows, which suggests a similar drifting offset, but no window's lag is separated from chance and the speed correlations are weak, so no clock can be fitted. The spikes of 489 end at 6255 s and its behaviour at 6218 s. None of the paper's findings on spike timing can be tested.

The dataset holds 2 of the paper's 19 animals (489 and 503), with units, trials and ball tracking. The other 11 ephys sessions, the 6 behaviour-only sessions, and the wall positions, whisker tracking, touch times and gait of any session are not in it, though the SI says the spikes of all filtered units are packaged with the behavioural data in one NWB file per animal. Twelve claims are blocked for these data.

In session 489 the trials table rows 1000 to 1610 (611 rows) all have start 3681.414 s, stop 3683.414 s and label OL_L_1.dat. The `trial` sample series gives them their own times (3683 to 6218 s), and they alternate between 305 two-second turns and 306 straight runs of 100 cm; 256 of the 305 turns go to the right.

In both sessions a run of OL rows (62 in 489, rows 173 to 757; 63 in 503, rows 251 to 777) has a stop time earlier than its start time. The samples of these rows carry timestamps that restart at the preceding straight row's start, so the sample timestamps go back in time (891 times in 489, 557 in 503); `ts_local` and the next row's start show that each lasted 2.0 s from its stated start.

The units tables hold 61 units for 489 and 43 for 503, where Table S1 gives 65 and 48. For 489, Fig. 5B gives 10 L2/3 and 13 L6 units, 43 FS and 22 RS; the file has 7, 12, 30 and 31. 503 has three units in a layer labelled WM, which the paper does not use.

Unit 101 of 489, which the paper calls 489101 and describes as RS (layer 5A in Fig. 4F and S10, 5B in Fig. S5E), is labelled Inhibitory in layer 5A with a 0.2 ms waveform, FS by the paper's 0.4 ms rule. It is the session's highest-rate unit, as the paper says of 489101.

The population rate of 489 averaged over its 61 units is 6.65 to 7.80 Hz in the second before the turn at any alignment of the spikes from -20 to 60 s, and 7.09 Hz over the whole recording, where the paper gives 2 ± 0.1 Hz for the same quantity (Fig. 1N).
The file of 489 gives the age as P63D, but its date of birth (2022-05-01) and session date (2022-07-08) are 68 days apart, the P68 of Table S1. Both files give a weight of 0.02 kg.

The paper's trial selections cannot be identified in the files. 489 has 249 and 251 labelled OL_L and OL_R trials where Fig. 1J-K uses 266 and 265 and Fig. S6A 520 OL_L; 503 has 230 and 283 where Fig. S4A uses 305 and 304 and Fig. 2A 414 in all. In 503 only 27.7% of trials are run above 10 cm/s (Table S1 52.8%; 37.0% of CL, 1.7% of OL_L and 31.8% of OL_R rows) and the mean running speed is 13.1 cm/s (16.1); all 513 OL trials give a success rate of 0.68, and the 94 run above 10 cm/s give 0.98 to 1.00, so the paper's figures may rest on a selection of running trials, or the deposited session of 503 may differ from the one analysed.

Several variables are not described. `distance_lat` and `distance_for` restart at 0 at each trial, and the sign of lateral distance (positive to the left) is not stated; `trial` has unit "n" and `ts_local` is the time since the trial started, neither described; the trial types are stimulus file names (`OL_L_1.dat`, `Straight 100cm A.dat`); `unit_type` (Excitatory, Inhibitory) is the waveform-duration classification, not a cell-type identification.

entries.name: 001341-armstrong-2026
entries.title: Barrel cortex activity during tactile VR navigation decisions (Armstrong and Vlasov 2026)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Armstrong and Vlasov (2026) on dandiset 001341, which holds two of the paper's 19 animals (489 and 503), with spike-sorted units, the trials table and the ball tracking. The behaviour is on the clock of the trials table and its claims are tested; the spike times are not, and the files hold no synchronisation signal, so the neural claims that need spike timing are blocked. Whisker, touch, wall and gait data are not in the dandiset.
